newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Deng's death halts talks on North Korean defector.
newsitem.headline: Deng's death halts talks on North Korean defector.

text.p: Talks on the fate of a senior North Korean defector stranded in South Korea's Beijing mission have been put on hold by the death of China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping, Seoul officials said on Thursday.
"China and South Korea share the same Asian tradition and you just don't want to disturb mourning people," a Seoul foreign ministry official said of the talks on defector Hwang Jang-yop.
"We will refrain from raising Hwang's issue with Chinese officials for the time being," he told Reuters.

Hwang, ranked 24th in Pyongyang's hierarchy, arrived at Seoul's consular office in Beijing with an aide on February 12, forcing China to tread a fine line between ideological ally North Korea and new business partner South Korea.
The Seoul official said a short-term delay in the talks over Hwang would not seriously affect his fate since his departure from Beijing was not imminent.

"Delay in our negotiations over Hwang appears inevitable but the process could be speeded up after Deng's funeral," the official said. China on Thursday declared six days of mourning for Deng, who died late on Wednesday.
Analysts said Deng's passing was the second dose of bad news for the North from Beijing in a week, following Hwang's flight.

"Relations between China and North Korea were held together by a feeling of solidarity between old revolutionaries. Deng was about the last of those revolutionaries," said Nozomu Akizuki, expert on northeast Asia at Japan's Meiji Gakuin University.

Another Seoul official said Hwang had videotaped confirmation of his defection and this had been passed to the Chinese government before signs emerged that North Korea might be ready to give up its fight to get Hwang back.

In the first indication of a change in its stance on Hwang's flight, Pyongyang's Foreign Ministry said late on Monday it would dismiss Hwang if he defected. Pyongyang had earlier been adamant in its claim that Hwang, the North's top ideologue, was kidnapped by South Korea.
Seoul officials said China might have shown Hwang's videotape to North Korea but added that there had been no significant progress in talks over Hwang.

"There had been two minor developments," Foreign Ministry spokesman Lee Kyu-hyung said. One was Pyongyang's softening of its stand and the second was China's announcement to its people for the first time on Wednesday that Hwang had entered the embassy of South Korea in Beijing.
China's official Xinhua news agency indicated Hwang had sought refuge in Seoul's mission of his own free will.
South Korea, in an apparent bid to encourage Pyongyang to end its Cold War confrontation with Seoul, announced on Thursday it would send $6 million in food aid to the North.

The aid, in response to the World Food Programme's appeal for $41.5 million to meet North Korea's food needs, will be in addition to the $3 million which Seoul contributed to a similar WFP aid programme last year.
The North's chronic food shortage has been worsened by devastating floods in the past two years.

"We hope this humanitarian gesture will help create a better atmosphere for the North to accept a briefing on peace talks on the Korean peninsula, although the food aid is not directly related to the issue," spokesman Lee said.
The North has twice postponed a briefing on the four-nation peace talks proposed jointly by South Korea and the United States last year. The talks also include China.
A Seoul government official said Pyongyang had hinted to Washington it could agree to the briefing early next month.
Hours before Seoul promised food aid to the North, the United States said it would send an extra $10 million in food aid following a $6.4 million contribution to the WFP in 1996.
